title: Virgo Cluster Galaxy NGC 4660
caption: Virgo cluster galaxy NGC 4660, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, and E. Peng (Peking University, Beijing)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble portrait shows NGC 4660, also cataloged as VCC 2000, one of 100 galaxies in the Virgo cluster that Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys examined for globular star clusters. The Virgo cluster, the nearest large galaxy cluster to Earth, contains over 2,000 galaxies and lies about 54 million light-years away.

Globular clusters are dense balls of hundreds of thousands of stars, and they contain some of the oldest stars still shining in the universe. Across the survey, Hubble identified more than 11,000 of them in Virgo, most older than 5 billion years. Its sharp vision separated these fuzzy clusters from stars in our own galaxy and from distant background galaxies, which is hard to do with telescopes on the ground.

The census suggests globulars form more readily where star birth is rapid and intense, rather than evenly from galaxy to galaxy. Dwarf galaxies close to Virgo's crowded center had surprisingly many globular clusters for their low masses, while dwarfs in the outskirts had fewer.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F475W (SDSS g) is shown in blue and F850LP (long pass z) in orange.
understand.eye: F850LP reaches into the near-infrared, beyond what the eye sees well, and the colors come from two separate filter images.

explore: Many of the globular clusters around M87, the giant elliptical galaxy at the center of Virgo, may have been taken from smaller galaxies that strayed too close. Astronomer Patrick Cote of the Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics said the results show that how efficiently star clusters form depends on their environment.
